Forest Attributes Analysis in R - ForestAR J. David Urquiza-Munoz 2026-03-23 Preface Are you ready to navigate the intersection of natural resources and computer science? This book is your guide to doing just that, equipping you with the essential skills to harness the power of data for forest management and conservation. More than just a collection of tools, this book provides a transparent and efficient approach to forestry informatics. Through a hands-on, project-based approach, youll learn to use the R programming languagea leading tool in data science and statistical analysis. You wont just be clicking buttons; youll be writing code to: - Import and manage diverse forest inventory data. - Clean and analyze complex datasets to reveal key insights. - Create stunning visualizations that tell a clear story about your data. By learning to use R command lines, youll master a workflow that is not only powerful but also reproducible. This scientific approach ensures that your work is transparent, easily shared, and builds a foundation of credibilitya vital skill for any modern forester or natural resource professional. By the end of this book, you will be prepared to tackle the complex challenges facing our forests, equipped with the computational thinking and data-driven skills demanded by the industry. About this book This short book should help you to get a better understanding of how the forest attributes analysis works, what you might want to consider in order to perform that are applicable for their respective purpose. 0.1 Render book You can render the HTML version of this example book without changing anything: Find the Build pane in the RStudio IDE, and Click on Build Book, then select your output format, or select All formats if youd like to use multiple formats from the same book source files. Or build the book from the R console: bookdown::render_book() To render this example to PDF as a bookdown::pdf_book, youll need to install XeLaTeX. You are recommended to install TinyTeX (which includes XeLaTeX): https://yihui.org/tinytex/. 0.2 Preview book As you work, you may start a local server to live preview this HTML book. This preview will update as you edit the book when you save individual .Rmd files. You can start the server in a work session by using the RStudio add-in Preview book, or from the R console: bookdown::serve_book()

2 Chapter 1: Introduction to Forest Data in R {#Chapter 1: Introduction to Forest Data in R} 2.1 1.1 Setting up the Environment 2.2 1.2 Importing the Inventory Data 2.3 1.3 Data Cleaning and Standardization 2.4 1.4 Exploring the Cleaned Data

2 Chapter 1: Introduction to Forest Data in R {#Chapter 1: Introduction to Forest Data in R} Welcome to the foundation of our forestry visualization journey. Before we can generate beautiful maps or 3D canopy models, we must first import and prepare our field data. R is uniquely powerful for this, as it allows us to document our data-cleaning steps transparently and reproducibly. In this chapter, we will set up our R environment, import our raw forest inventory data, and perform basic cleaning to ensure it is ready for spatial and statistical analysis. 2.1 1.1 Setting up the Environment To work effectively with forestry data, we need a specific set of tools. The tidyverse is a collection of R packages designed for data science (providing tools for reading, manipulating, and visualizing data), while sf (Simple Features) is the modern standard for handling spatial data in R. Lets load our primary packages. # Install packages if you haven't already: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "sf", "knitr")) library(tidyverse) library(sf) library(knitr) # Used for rendering neat tables in our book 2.2 1.2 Importing the Inventory Data Forestry data collected in the field often comes in various formats. Our dataset is a CSV file, but like many datasets generated in South America or Europe, it uses a semicolon (;) to separate columns instead of a comma. We must explicitly tell R how to read this specific format using the sep argument. # Import the raw data raw_inventory <- read.csv("data/inventory.csv", sep = ";", dec = ".", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) # Check the dimensions of our dataset (number of rows and columns) dim(raw_inventory) ## [1] 693 15 2.3 1.3 Data Cleaning and Standardization Raw field data rarely comes perfectly formatted for analysis. Column names might include spaces, special characters, or abbreviations that are hard to remember. Lets clean our dataset by renaming the most critical columns to standard English forestry terms and selecting only the variables we need for our upcoming visualizations. inventory_clean <- raw_inventory %>% # Rename columns for easier coding later rename( Plot_ID = SP, Tree_ID = Nro.Arb, Common_Name = NOMBRE.VULGAR, Scientific_Name = NOMBRE.CIENTIFICO, DBH_cm = DAP, Height_m =HT, Easting = ESTE, Northing = NORTE ) %>% # Keep only the columns relevant for our visual analysis select(Plot_ID, Tree_ID, Common_Name, Scientific_Name, DBH_cm, Height_m,Easting, Northing) %>% # Filter out any rows that might be missing critical spatial or size data filter(!is.na(DBH_cm), !is.na(Easting), !is.na(Northing)) 2.4 1.4 Exploring the Cleaned Data Before moving on to complex visualizations, it is good practice to visually inspect the first few rows of our cleaned dataset to ensure our import and manipulation steps worked correctly. # Display the first 5 rows as a polished table kable(head(inventory_clean, 5), caption = "Table 1.1: Preview of the cleaned forest inventory dataset.") 3 Chapter 2: Forest Composition & Structure 3.1 2.1 Species Composition 3.2 2.2 Forest Stand Structure (DBH)

3 Chapter 2: Forest Composition & Structure With our inventory data cleaned and standardized, we can now explore the ecological characteristics of our forest stand. Two of the most fundamental questions in any forest inventory are: What species are growing here? and How big are they? In this chapter, we will use the ggplot2 package (which is loaded automatically with tidyverse) to create clear, publication-ready visualizations of our forests composition and structure. 3.1 2.1 Species Composition Tropical and Neotropical forests are incredibly diverse. Visualizing the abundance of every single species in a single chart can result in a cluttered and unreadable mess. Instead, a standard practice is to isolate and visualize the most dominant species to understand the primary makeup of the canopy. Lets calculate the top 10 most abundant species in our dataset and create a horizontal bar chart. # Calculate species frequencies and filter for the top 10 top_species <- inventory_clean %>% count(Scientific_Name, name = "Count") %>% arrange(desc(Count)) %>% slice_max(order_by = Count, n = 10) # Create a horizontal bar chart ggplot(top_species, aes(x = reorder(Scientific_Name, Count), y = Count)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.8) + coord_flip() + # Flips the axes for easier reading of species names labs( title = "Dominant Species in the Forest Stand", x = "Scientific Name", y = "Number of Individuals" ) + theme_minimal() + theme( axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic") # Standard practice: italicize scientific names ) Figure 3.1: Top 10 most abundant tree species in the inventory. 3.2 2.2 Forest Stand Structure (DBH) The distribution of tree diameters is a key indicator of forest health, history, and successional stage. In natural, uneven-aged forests, we typically expect to see a Reverse-J curve. This means there are many small, young trees in the understory and progressively fewer large, older trees forming the upper canopy. We can visualize this using a histogram of our DBH_cm (Diameter at Breast Height) column. ggplot(inventory_clean, aes(x = DBH_cm)) + # We use a binwidth of 5 cm, which is standard for forestry DBH classes geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "forestgreen", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) + # Create dynamic x-axis breaks based on our actual data max scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max(inventory_clean$DBH_cm, na.rm = TRUE), by = 10)) + labs( title = "Diameter Distribution of the Stand", subtitle = "The Reverse-J shape indicates an uneven-aged, regenerating forest", x = "Diameter at Breast Height (cm)", y = "Frequency (Number of Trees)" ) + theme_minimal() Figure 3.2: Diameter distribution showing a classic Reverse-J curve for a natural forest.

5 Parts You can add parts to organize one or more book chapters together. Parts can be inserted at the top of an .Rmd file, before the first-level chapter heading in that same file. Add a numbered part: # (PART) Act one {-} (followed by # A chapter) Add an unnumbered part: # (PART\*) Act one {-} (followed by # A chapter) Add an appendix as a special kind of un-numbered part: # (APPENDIX) Other stuff {-} (followed by # A chapter). Chapters in an appendix are prepended with letters instead of numbers.

7 Blocks 7.1 Equations Here is an equation. \[\begin{equation} f\left(k\right) = \binom{n}{k} p^k\left(1-p\right)^{n-k} \tag{7.1} \end{equation}\] You may refer to using \@ref(eq:binom), like see Equation (7.1). 7.2 Theorems and proofs Labeled theorems can be referenced in text using \@ref(thm:tri), for example, check out this smart theorem 7.1. Theorem 7.1 For a right triangle, if \(c\) denotes the length of the hypotenuse and \(a\) and \(b\) denote the lengths of the other two sides, we have \[a^2 + b^2 = c^2\] Read more here https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/markdown-extensions-by-bookdown.html. 7.3 Callout blocks The bs4_book theme also includes special callout blocks, like this .rmdnote. You can use markdown inside a block. head(beaver1, n = 5) ## day time temp activ ## 1 346 840 36.33 0 ## 2 346 850 36.34 0 ## 3 346 900 36.35 0 ## 4 346 910 36.42 0 ## 5 346 920 36.55 0 It is up to the user to define the appearance of these blocks for LaTeX output. 9 Cross-references 9.1 Chapters and sub-chapters 9.2 Captioned figures and tables

9 Cross-references Cross-references make it easier for your readers to find and link to elements in your book. 9.1 Chapters and sub-chapters There are two steps to cross-reference any heading: Label the heading: # Hello world {#nice-label}. Leave the label off if you like the automated heading generated based on your heading title: for example, # Hello world = # Hello world {#hello-world}. To label an un-numbered heading, use: # Hello world {-#nice-label} or {# Hello world .unnumbered}. Next, reference the labeled heading anywhere in the text using \@ref(nice-label); for example, please see Chapter 9. If you prefer text as the link instead of a numbered reference use: any text you want can go here. 9.2 Captioned figures and tables Figures and tables with captions can also be cross-referenced from elsewhere in your book using \@ref(fig:chunk-label) and \@ref(tab:chunk-label), respectively. See Figure 9.1. par(mar = c(4, 4, .1, .1)) plot(pressure, type = 'b', pch = 19) Figure 9.1: Here is a nice figure!
